title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: Latency
summary: Latency is the time elapsed between a request being initiated by a client and the corresponding response being received, measured end-to-end and typically reported as percentiles (p50, p90, p99, p99.9) rather than averages.
objectives: Why are latency percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9) more useful than averages?
What is tail-latency amplification, and how do you mitigate it?
Explain the latency-vs-throughput trade-off using Little's Law.
What are the main sources of latency in a distributed system, and how do you mitigate each?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Latency is the time elapsed between a request being initiated by a client and the corresponding response being received, measured end-to-end and typically reported as percentiles (p50, p90, p99, p99.9) rather than averages.

Latency is the user-visible performance metric — the one customers actually feel. Every other system design property (availability, scalability, durability) is invisible if it works correctly; latency is the property users perceive on every single interaction. The famous Amazon finding — a 100ms increase in page load time reduced sales by 1% — is often quoted because it makes latency concrete in business terms. Google's similar finding — a 400ms delay in search results reduced searches by 0.59% — and Akamai's finding that 100ms of latency reduces mobile conversion by 7% underscore the same point: latency directly affects revenue, engagement, and retention. Senior engineers treat latency as a first-class SLO, not a side effect of "performance."

The first non-obvious lesson about latency is that averages lie. The mean of [10ms, 10ms, 10ms, 10ms, 1000ms] is 208ms, but that single 1000ms request represents a user who saw a frozen page for a second — a very different experience from "everything is 208ms." Production systems report latency as percentiles: p50 (median), p90, p99, p99.9. p50 tells you the typical user experience; p99 tells you the experience of the slowest 1% of users, which on a high-traffic site may be thousands or millions of users per day. For a service handling 1 billion requests/day, p99.9 represents 1 million requests — even the "long tail" matters at scale. The gap between p50 and p99 is also informative: a service with p50=10ms and p99=2000ms has a tail-latency problem, often caused by GC pauses, lock contention, network jitter, or background processes stealing CPU. A service with p50=100ms and p99=120ms is well-behaved.

Tail latency amplification is the most important and counterintuitive phenomenon in distributed-system latency. If a single backend has p99=100ms, you might expect a service that calls 10 such backends in parallel to also have p99≈100ms (since the slowest of 10 dominates). But the math is brutal: the probability that all 10 backends are fast is (0.99)^10 ≈ 0.904, meaning 9.6% of requests see at least one slow backend. The p99 of the parallel call is now the worst-case latency of any backend, often 5-10x the individual p99. With 100 backends, (0.99)^100 ≈ 0.366 — two-thirds of requests see at least one slow call. This is why Google's Jeff Dean has written extensively about tail-tolerant system design: at scale, you must assume every request will see at least one slow component, and you must architect so that one slow component does not dominate the user experience. Techniques include hedged requests (send a second request after a delay and use whichever returns first), bounding request fan-out, and aggressively caching slow dependencies.

Latency comes from four main sources, each requiring different mitigations. Network latency is the speed-of-light round-trip plus router hops — a US-to-Europe round-trip is ~80ms minimum, and cross-Pacific is ~150ms. CDN edge caching and geographic deployment are the only real fixes; you cannot beat the speed of light. Queueing latency occurs when requests wait in a queue for a busy server — the M/M/1 queueing formula `W = ρ/(μ-λ)` shows that as utilization approaches 100%, wait time explodes non-linearly. The fix is to keep servers below 70-80% utilization and use adaptive load shedding. Processing latency is the time the CPU spends doing the actual work — parsing, computing, serializing. Profile-guided optimization, algorithmic improvements, and using faster languages (Rust, C++ for hot paths) are the typical fixes. Garbage collection latency is the JVM's stop-the-world pauses, which can stall a service for tens of milliseconds to seconds. Tuning GC (ZGC, Shenandoah), reducing allocation, and using off-heap storage mitigate this. Each source has different signatures in metrics, and the right fix depends on identifying which source dominates.

The latency-vs-throughput trade-off is one of the foundational tensions in system design. Throughput is requests per second; latency is the time per request. They are related but not equivalent: a system can have high throughput (many concurrent slow requests) and high latency, or low throughput (few concurrent fast requests) and low latency. The relationship is captured by Little's Law: `L = λW`, where L is the number of in-flight requests, λ is throughput, and W is latency. At low utilization, latency is dominated by the work itself (service time); at high utilization, latency is dominated by queueing wait time, which grows non-linearly as utilization approaches 100%. This is why production systems target 70-80% CPU utilization — beyond that, latency degrades sharply even before throughput peaks. Batching is the classic trade-off lever: batching many small requests into one large request improves throughput dramatically but adds latency (waiting for the batch to fill). Kafka and database bulk inserts use this trade-off; the right batch size depends on whether the workload is latency-sensitive (smaller batches) or throughput-sensitive (larger batches).

The real-world canonical example is Amazon's latency engineering. Amazon has publicly shared that 100ms of additional latency on the product page reduces conversion by 1%, and the entire Amazon architecture is shaped by this finding. CDN edge caching puts product images and static assets within ~10ms of every user. DynamoDB was built explicitly to provide single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale, using SSDs, consistent hashing, and request routing that puts the partition leader close to the data. The Amazon product page is assembled from dozens of microservices in parallel, with strict per-service latency budgets — a service that exceeds its budget is called out in dashboards and is a candidate for replacement or caching. Amazon's "two-pizza team" structure gives each team ownership of a service with explicit SLOs, including latency SLOs that are tracked and enforced. The lesson: latency is not an accident of fast hardware; it is the result of architectural choices that prioritize it.

The second real-world example is Google's tail-latency engineering for Search. Google has published research (Dean & Barroso, "The Tail at Scale") describing how Google handles the reality that at scale, every user request sees at least one slow component. Their techniques include hedged requests (send a backup request after 10ms if the original hasn't returned, cancel the loser), micro-partitioning (split data into thousands of small partitions so each request touches many partitions in parallel and the slowest dominates), and "tail-tolerant" algorithms that can complete correctly even if some replicas are slow. Google's published SLO for Search includes a strict p99 latency target, and the entire infrastructure — from the network fabric to the storage layer to the query engine — is designed to keep p99 low. The key insight: at Google scale (billions of queries/day), p99 represents millions of queries, and even the tail must be fast. The pitfall for smaller systems: copying Google's architecture blindly is overkill. The right approach is to understand the principles (percentile measurement, tail amplification, hedging) and apply them only where the workload justifies the complexity.

Latency connects to every other system design concept. It is constrained by scalability — as load increases, queueing grows and latency rises. It is constrained by availability — a slow response is often indistinguishable from a failure. It is constrained by fault tolerance — circuit breakers and timeouts trade latency for resilience. It is constrained by cost — lower latency typically requires more replicas, more geographic distribution, more caching, all of which cost money. Senior engineers treat latency as a budget: each layer of the stack gets a portion of the total user-perceived latency, and exceeding the budget anywhere breaks the overall SLO. Latency budgets cascade: if the frontend allows 200ms total, the API layer gets 150ms, the database gets 50ms, and the network between them gets 20ms. Exceeding any budget forces a redesign or a renegotiation of the total. The discipline of latency budgeting is what separates systems that feel fast from systems that feel sluggish, and it is one of the most important skills in senior system design.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Client] -->|network RTT 30ms| B[Edge CDN]
    B -->|cache hit 5ms| C[Response]
    B -->|cache miss| D[Origin LB]
    D -->|1ms| E[API Gateway]
    E -->|queue wait 5ms| F[App Server]
    F -->|GC pause 50ms?| G[Business Logic]
    G -->|10ms| H[DB Primary]
    H -->|5ms| I[(Storage)]
    I --> C

    subgraph "Latency Sources"
        J[Network 30ms]
        K[Queue 5ms]
        L[GC 0-50ms]
        M[Processing 10ms]
        N[Storage 5ms]
    end
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
Client request timeline (p50 vs p99):

  p50:   |--net 30--|--queue 2--|--cpu 10--|--db 5--| = 47ms
  p99:   |--net 30--|--queue 20--|--GC 50--|--cpu 10--|--db 5--| = 115ms
                              ^           ^
                              |           |
                          tail source   tail source

  Tail-latency amplification (parallel fan-out 10x):

  Single call:     p99 = 100ms
  10 parallel:     p99 = ~600ms   (P(at least 1 slow) = 1 - 0.99^10 = 9.6%)
  100 parallel:    p99 = ~1000ms  (P(at least 1 slow) = 1 - 0.99^100 = 63%)

  Hedged request mitigates:
  Send call #1 -> wait 20ms -> send call #2 -> use first response
  Effective p99 drops to ~50ms (whichever replica is faster)
```

### Walkthrough
1. The client initiates a request. Network round-trip to the nearest CDN edge is typically 5–30ms depending on geography; this is irreducible speed-of-light latency.
2. The CDN checks its cache. A hit returns within 1–5ms; a miss forwards to the origin, adding another 20–50ms.
3. The request reaches the API gateway, which authenticates, rate-limits, and routes. This adds 1–5ms but can spike if the gateway queues requests during high load.
4. The application server processes the request. Typical CPU time is 5–20ms, but JVM GC pauses can add 10–500ms to the p99. The server may call downstream services, each contributing their own latency.
5. The database executes the query. A well-indexed lookup is 1–5ms; a complex join or a lock-contended write can be 50–500ms. The response travels back through the same layers, doubling the one-way latency.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Latency percentile calculator and tail-amplification simulator.
- Compute the p-th percentile (p in [0, 100]) using nearest-rank.
- Print a full latency percentile report.
- Simulate per-call latencies: 99% fast, 1% slow (mimics GC pauses, etc.).
- Slow calls have wide distribution
- Fast calls are tightly clustered
- Sample `fanout` calls in parallel, take the max (slowest dominates)
- If first returns before hedge_delay, use it

**Defines:** `percentile()`, `latency_report()`, `simulate_request()`, `fanout_latency()`, `hedged_latency()`

```python
"""
Latency percentile calculator and tail-amplification simulator.
Takes a list of request latencies and prints p50/p90/p99/p99.9.
Also simulates how parallel fan-out amplifies tail latency.
"""
import random
import statistics
from typing import List

def percentile(data: List[float], p: float) -> float:
    """Compute the p-th percentile (p in [0, 100]) using nearest-rank."""
    if not data:
        raise ValueError("empty data")
    sorted_data = sorted(data)
    n = len(sorted_data)
    # Nearest-rank method
    rank = max(1, int(round(p / 100.0 * n)))
    return sorted_data[min(rank, n) - 1]

def latency_report(latencies: List[float], label: str = ""):
    """Print a full latency percentile report."""
    if not latencies:
        print(f"{label}: no data")
        return
    print(f"--- Latency Report: {label} ---")
    print(f"  count  : {len(latencies)}")
    print(f"  mean   : {statistics.mean(latencies):.2f} ms")
    print(f"  p50    : {percentile(latencies, 50):.2f} ms")
    print(f"  p90    : {percentile(latencies, 90):.2f} ms")
    print(f"  p95    : {percentile(latencies, 95):.2f} ms")
    print(f"  p99    : {percentile(latencies, 99):.2f} ms")
    print(f"  p99.9  : {percentile(latencies, 99.9):.2f} ms")
    print(f"  max    : {max(latencies):.2f} ms")
    print(f"  p99/p50: {percentile(latencies, 99) / percentile(latencies, 50):.2f}x")
    print()

def simulate_request(num_calls: int = 10000, slow_fraction: float = 0.01,
                     fast_ms: float = 10.0, slow_ms: float = 200.0) -> List[float]:
    """Simulate per-call latencies: 99% fast, 1% slow (mimics GC pauses, etc.)."""
    latencies = []
    for _ in range(num_calls):
        if random.random() < slow_fraction:
            # Slow calls have wide distribution
            lat = slow_ms + random.uniform(-50, 300)
        else:
            # Fast calls are tightly clustered
            lat = fast_ms + random.uniform(-3, 5)
        latencies.append(max(0.1, lat))
    return latencies

def fanout_latency(call_latencies: List[float], fanout: int,
                   samples: int = 10000) -> List[float]:
    """Simulate parallel fan-out: latency = max of `fanout` random calls."""
    combined = []
    for _ in range(samples):
        # Sample `fanout` calls in parallel, take the max (slowest dominates)
        chosen = [random.choice(call_latencies) for _ in range(fanout)]
        combined.append(max(chosen))
    return combined

def hedged_latency(call_latencies: List[float], hedge_delay: float = 20.0,
                   samples: int = 10000) -> List[float]:
    """Simulate hedged request: send 2nd request after hedge_delay, take min."""
    result = []
    for _ in range(samples):
        a = random.choice(call_latencies)
        b = random.choice(call_latencies)
        # If first returns before hedge_delay, use it
        if a <= hedge_delay:
            result.append(a)
        else:
            # Otherwise send a hedge at hedge_delay; use whichever returns first
            # b starts at hedge_delay, so effective_b = hedge_delay + b
            effective_b = hedge_delay + b
            result.append(min(a, effective_b))
    return result

if __name__ == "__main__":
    random.seed(42)

    # 1. Single-service latency profile
    single = simulate_request(num_calls=100000, slow_fraction=0.01)
    latency_report(single, "Single backend (p99=200ms)")

    # 2. Fan-out amplification
    for fanout in [1, 5, 10, 50, 100]:
        combined = fanout_latency(single, fanout=fanout, samples=50000)
        p50 = percentile(combined, 50)
        p99 = percentile(combined, 99)
        prob_slow = 1 - (0.99 ** fanout)
        print(f"Fan-out={fanout:3d}: p50={p50:6.1f}ms  p99={p99:6.1f}ms  "
              f"P(>=1 slow)={prob_slow*100:5.1f}%")
    print()

    # 3. Hedged request mitigation
    hedged = hedged_latency(single, hedge_delay=20.0, samples=50000)
    latency_report(hedged, "With hedged requests (delay=20ms)")

    # 4. Demonstrate averages lie
    pathological = [10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 1000]
    print("Pathological sample:", pathological)
    print(f"  mean = {statistics.mean(pathological):.1f}")
    print(f"  p50  = {percentile(pathological, 50):.1f}")
    print(f"  p99  = {percentile(pathological, 99):.1f}")
    print("  -> mean hides the 1000ms outlier; percentiles expose it.")
```

Percentiles expose the distribution: p50=10ms tells you the typical experience; p99=1000ms tells you the worst 1% experience; p99.9 tells you the worst 0.1%.
